title: Bold outside, careful inside
hook: be confident about outside things and cautious about your own judgments (Discourses 2.1)

segments.voice: Yesterday: stand firm, roots holding while the branches move. Where did you stay steady under pressure? Day four hundred seven.

Hunters in the ancient world had a clever trick for catching deer. They'd string a line of feathers across the woods. The feathers fluttered, the deer panicked and ran the other way, straight into the nets the hunters had set. The deer weren't cowards. They were afraid of the wrong thing, and fearless about the wrong thing. Epictetus thought most of us live exactly like those deer. Today: bold outside, careful inside.
screen: `A LINE OF FEATHERS.` → `THE DEER RUN INTO THE NETS.` → `AFRAID OF THE WRONG THING.`

segments.voice: This opens book two of the Discourses, chapter one: that confidence isn't at odds with caution. The Stoics claimed you should be both, completely bold and completely careful, and people thought that sounded like nonsense. Epictetus explains. Be careful, he says, where the real danger is: in your own will. That's where you can actually go wrong, by agreeing too fast, wanting the wrong thing, acting on a bad impression. And be bold about everything outside the will, because nothing out there can make you bad. Then he shows how we flip it. We're terrified of things outside us: death, exile, pain, losing face. And we're reckless inside: careless with our judgments, quick to agree with any thought that comes along. Like the deer, fleeing the feathers and running into the nets. Epictetus has another image for the outside fears. Death and pain, he says, are like the masks that scare little children. Turn the mask around and look at the back. It doesn't bite. What frightens us is mostly our opinion about death and pain, not the things themselves. This doesn't mean being careless with your health or your safety; Epictetus would still have you look both ways crossing the street. It means putting your carefulness where it does the most good, on your own judgments, and letting your courage go out into the world.
screen: `BOTH BOLD AND CAREFUL.` · `CAREFUL WHERE THE REAL DANGER IS.` · `WE FLIP IT, LIKE THE DEER.` · `TURN THE MASK AROUND.` · then, large: `BOLD OUTSIDE, CAREFUL INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Sit and breathe. Think of one outside thing you've been avoiding out of fear: a phone call, a conversation, applying for something, speaking up. Look at it like a mask, and turn it around. What's actually on the back? Usually it's discomfort, not disaster. Then turn inward and notice one place you've been careless: a judgment you made too fast, an assumption you never checked. Hold both. Bold out there, careful in here. The bell holds the time.
Bold outside. Epictetus' answer to the Stoic paradox: be confident about what's outside your will, and save your caution for your own judgments.
Your line: bold outside, careful inside. Today, be bold about one outside thing you've been dodging, and careful with one judgment before you act on it. Day four hundred seven.

howItsDone: Stoic readers often use this chapter to sort their fears, acting boldly on outside things they've been avoiding while slowing down their own quick judgments.

fork.setup: you're a deer in the woods. a line of feathers flutters ahead of you. what do the deer in Epictetus' story do?
options: flee the feathers and run into the nets.
fork.reveal: they fear the harmless feathers and run straight into the real danger, the way we fear outside things and grow careless within.

original.note: Greek tharsos: confidence, boldness; paired in Discourses 2.1 with eulabeia, caution.

trapdoor: what you thought: be brave and don't overthink.
what it means: be brave about outside things, and careful with your own judgments, where the real danger is.
what a scholar hears: the 'bold and cautious' paradox was a Stoic teaching critics mocked, and 2.1 is Epictetus' defense of it, using the Roman hunter's feather line.

sources.ref: Discourses 2.1 (that confidence is not inconsistent with caution)

notes: Discourses 2.1 paraphrased: confidence about things outside the will, caution about things within; deer fleeing feathers into the nets; death and pain as masks (mormolykeia) that frighten children. Confirm.
The feather line (Latin formido) as a hunting device is attested in Roman sources (e.g. Virgil, Seneca); confirm before keeping 'Roman hunter's feather line' in the trapdoor.
